clock: the computer that ran the builder (UK time on Richard's PC)

rule.bands: A above 90%; B+ above 82.5% to 90%; B above 75% to 82.5%; C+ above 66.67% to 75%; C above 58.33% to 66.67%; C- above 50% to 58.33%; D above 25% to 50%; F up to 25%
rule.rank: percentile rank = (scores below + half the ties) / population size; the population of an item is every stock holding a score on that item from its registered run (or its published memo)
rule.registered_run: the newest live card in the conveyor's trays whose run holds scores; dry, cancelled and control runs never enter
rule.boundaries: per item, the lowest score that earned each grade today; null where no score earned that grade
rule.comparison_set: the stocks analysed by the new approach (the Sets of Questions/Items approach)
rule.fixed_letters: on memo topics 5, 6, 8, 11 and 12 a cell carrying fixed_letter shows the Rater's own letter from a real-world measure (A to F, no sub-grade), never re-cut; its rank and p are information only (D-SQ-267, D-SQ-271)
rule.fixed_cutoffs: v1.5 (his Messages 427 and 428; D-SQ-280): three letter rules, one per item, stated in each item's letter_rule. RANK within the population of stocks scored on the same scale (A top 10%; B next 15%, B+ its top half; C next 25% in thirds C+, C, C-; D next 25%; F bottom 25%) for the judgement items. His FIXED CUT-OFFS on the number (A 90 and above; B+ 82.5 to 89; B 75 to 82.4; C+ 66.67 to 74; C 58.33 to 66.66; C- 50 to 58.32; D 25 to 49; F below 25) for the items where 50 means neither positive nor negative: topics 1 and 2, Thesis's Change Forces' Strength, the External change forces and Internal change forces group judgements and their questions. The Rater's letter from his cut-offs on the MEASURE for topics 6, 8, 11 and 12, the number placed inside the letter's band. Rank and the percentile stay on every cell for information.
rule.scales: v1.5: every cell carries scale_tag; a rank letter is cut only among cells of the same scale (rater-v3 = the Rater v3.0 after the memo; rater-v2 and rater-v1-keyed = earlier Raters; writer-1.9 = the Investment Analyst's own score as it wrote the answer, the old method; writer-memo = the memo Analyst's own topic score). Old-method cells are labelled and stay until the Rater scores that stock's memo.
rule.scale_caveat: scores tagged rater-v1-keyed were set by the Rater of 1-Nov-26, whose key put 50 at the typical listed European company but was anchored on effect size rather than on percentiles; scores tagged rater-v2 or rater-v3 are standings in the Universe.

M:topic:1.scale_version: the Rater v3.0, 2026-11-03: standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10), every item scored after the memo is written, the case first on judgement topics, anchors from the corrected ordering of 75 companies, the question groups' keys (D-SQ-280)
M:topic:1.note: set by the Rater; the Investment Analyst's own score was 46
M:topic:1.letter_rule: rank within this item's population of the same scale (A top 10%, B next 15%, C, D and F quarters; B+, B, C+, C, C- sub-grades)
M:topic:1.reason: One strong, dated, law-backed tailwind (Dutch grid capex rising from about EUR 10bn to 18bn a year, permit-free substations from late 2027, the SF6 ban Alfen is already certified for) reaches only the grid unit, about 45% of revenue. It comes as volume only, rationed by the operators' technicians and permits (two of three installed 20-30% below plan in 2025), and three monopsony buyers hold its price. Against it, structural headwinds (cell makers selling turnkey, a renewed price war, VAT-rebate removal, charging prices in their seventh quarter of decline as value moves to site owners) act on the two units that make about 60% of gross profit. Consensus sales growth at the 80th percentile reflects the grid volume, but external forces give no support to group margin, so the net is slightly negative over two to three years: negative to mid-2027, mildly positive after. I am a touch above the External change forces group's 44 because the grid force is unusually well funded and dated.

M:topic:5.scale_version: the Rater v3.0, 2026-11-03: standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10), every item scored after the memo is written, the case first on judgement topics, anchors from the corrected ordering of 75 companies, the question groups' keys (D-SQ-280)
M:topic:5.note: set by the Rater; the Investment Analyst's own score was 62
M:topic:5.letter_rule: rank within this item's population of the same scale (A top 10%, B next 15%, C, D and F quarters; B+, B, C+, C, C- sub-grades)
M:topic:5.reason: This scores the structure. Operating leverage is real and proven both ways: a 26-27% contribution margin on about EUR 100m of largely personnel opex, plus EUR 23-24m of fixed charges below EBITDA, so 10% more or less revenue moves EBITDA 40-50% (the same EUR 440m of revenue gave 18% EBITDA in FY22 and 5.9% in FY25). The other gears are absent or negative: prices fall in charging, follow cells in storage and are capped in grid; there is no financial leverage; the big cost-out is already in the base; and the feedback loops run mostly negative. Opex inflation also eats about a third of the drop-through, so the forecast EPS-to-revenue ratio from a near-zero base overstates the gearing. That is above the level-50 mix on gearing alone, but well short of Judges Scientific's 72-type proven leverage with stable pricing.

M:topic:8.reason: The two measures are mixed on their face (C), but I move the letter one step to D because the parts strongly contradict the 59th-percentile sell-side score: FY2027 EPS flat over three months and down 3% over twelve, target prices down 8% in three months, the Buy share down 17 points, narrative negative since September, and the price below its 150- and 200-day averages with the 200-day falling for twelve months; guidance gives no momentum by construction and peers (AddLife positive) cannot lift it. Placed in the lower half of D because relative strength sits on the edge of the bottom fifth.

M:topic:9.scale_version: the Rater v3.0, 2026-11-03: standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10), every item scored after the memo is written, the case first on judgement topics, anchors from the corrected ordering of 75 companies, the question groups' keys (D-SQ-280)
M:topic:9.note: set by the Rater; the Investment Analyst's own score was 50.0
M:topic:9.letter_rule: rank within this item's population of the same scale (A top 10%, B next 15%, C, D and F quarters; B+, B, C+, C, C- sub-grades)
M:topic:9.reason: The operating case is simple and trackable (revenue plus or minus 2%, 2027 EPS SEK 3.20-3.80, about -10% to +7%, non-cyclical demand, one swing variable and three dated tests), but the equity outcome is binary on one document: a 10-20% chance of an accounting event costing 20-35% on the shares, a fair trough 30-37% below, 2.4x leverage with SEK 645m-1,050m of earn-outs outside net debt, a thin register exposed to a short report, and undated device-line and insurer losses. Narrower in earnings than IMCD but with a more binary equity event, between OMV Petrom's sudden fiscal risk and Fevertree's flattered risk, coherent with Risks groups of 36 and 48.

M:topic:10.reason: The computed Broadening is wrong and the memo's Bottoming is right: momentum is F with the 200-day falling, revisions to EPS and cash are negative and due to fall further, the multiple is at the 9th percentile of its history, and the dated conditions for a turn (FY2026 cash flow and inventory in February 2027, the annual report by April 2027) have not yet arrived, with a 'false friend' path to Collapsing if cash disappoints again. M:topic:1.reason: The external forces take from growth and margins over two to three years: beer about two-thirds of volume and structurally flat (footprint +0.3% a year, Western Europe -4% in H1 and Q3 2026), China volume -6% and -10% in the quarters that carry two-thirds of its profit with part of the loss share and channel, rule-driven mainstream price competition in the UK and Poland, dated regulation (Vietnamese excise, UK deposit scheme and sugar threshold) and a 2027 input-cost round of about 160bp of gross margin; the real external positives (soft drinks and alcohol-free growth, India, easy Chinese comparatives from Q2 2027, inflation-linked price pass-through in a rational oligopoly) only partly offset, and the PepsiCo licence wins and the Kazakhstan volume are the company's own and scored in topic 2. Consensus sales growth at the 31st percentile fits a clearly but not severely negative environment, just below Entra's mild negative and above Vodafone's, coherent with the External change forces group at 35.

M:topic:2.reason: A broad, resourced and largely delivered programme: Britvic closed and its synergies running ahead (about 30% in year one against 10-15%, target raised to GBP 110m), Southeast Asia's 25% sold at 21.3x EBIT, the Kazakhstan plant opened on schedule, PepsiCo territories added, the executive team rebuilt and leverage cut from 3.9x to 3.0x in a year, which together take EPS growth from about 3% a year to about 8% with a dated buyback ahead; it is held back by Britvic earning below its cost of capital (about 5-7%), earnings quality in transition (DKK 1.9bn of special items, the hybrid, rising minorities), weaker working capital and a revenue algorithm never met, and the self-help fades after 2027. I place it a little above the Internal change forces group's 64 because whether the effect is already in consensus belongs to topic 7, not here; it sits between OEM International's acquisition-led change and Theon's growth pivot.

M:topic:1.scale_version: the Rater v3.0, 2026-11-03: standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10), every item scored after the memo is written, the case first on judgement topics, anchors from the corrected ordering of 75 companies, the question groups' keys (D-SQ-280)
M:topic:1.note: set by the Rater; the Investment Analyst's own score was 50.0
M:topic:1.letter_rule: rank within this item's population of the same scale (A top 10%, B next 15%, C, D and F quarters; B+, B, C+, C, C- sub-grades)
M:topic:1.reason: External forces net to about zero for 18 months and slightly negative after: real fibre and postpaid demand, Greek GDP near 2%, pro-OTE regulation (FTTC stop-sell, sector taxes gone, cheaper spectrum renewals) and inflation feeding the price clause, against the RRF ending in December 2026, energy hedge cover falling to about 66% and the Vodafone-PPC venture plus a 10-13% wholesale tariff cut eroding the 80-85%-margin national wholesale layer (the fast-migration tail is scored in topic 9). The clause itself is scored in topic 2; the -0.1% consensus sales growth (5.9th percentile) reflects the zero-margin transit exit rather than the environment; as Richard ruled, this is a slight net negative in the 40s, not an F, and below internal forces, matching the group's 47, between Tenaris and Carlsberg.

M:topic:2.scale_version: the Rater v3.0, 2026-11-03: standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10), every item scored after the memo is written, the case first on judgement topics, anchors from the corrected ordering of 75 companies, the question groups' keys (D-SQ-280)
M:topic:2.note: set by the Rater; the Investment Analyst's own score was 55.0
M:topic:2.letter_rule: rank within this item's population of the same scale (A top 10%, B next 15%, C, D and F quarters; B+, B, C+, C, C- sub-grades)
M:topic:2.reason: A decisive change now 28 months old (new CEO, Romania sold, 300 EURm transit exited, rural fibre concession, indirect costs from 31% to 28% of service revenue, A- rating, a 70-100% payout) is delivered and in the margin and cash, and what is left is about 1-2% of EBITDA a year of execution, the latent annual price clause and a smoothed distribution, against slowing mobile growth, adjusted EBITDAaL that excludes voluntary-leave charges, and no mid-term targets or balance-sheet use. In line with Richard's ruling it is a gentle positive in the C band, like his CVS Group 55 (positive but not getting more ambitious); just above ASML, whose internal leg is similar in size, and below Odfjell's earnings-adding deal, coherent with the group's 57.

M:topic:3.scale_version: the Rater v3.0, 2026-11-03: standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10), every item scored after the memo is written, the case first on judgement topics, anchors from the corrected ordering of 75 companies, the question groups' keys (D-SQ-280)
M:topic:3.note: set by the Rater; the Investment Analyst's own score was 72.0
M:topic:3.letter_rule: rank within this item's population of the same scale (A top 10%, B next 15%, C, D and F quarters; B+, B, C+, C, C- sub-grades)
M:topic:3.reason: Qualitatively strong: a three-player market where OTE takes 73% of the EBITDA pool and 93% of operating free cash flow, rivals that cannot fund a price war, retail moats that widen with each fibre migration, and a capable operator-CEO; held back by a small 2-4% nominal market, state-granted protections, a wholesale moat now narrowing, minimum governance and low returns on new fibre capital until copper is switched off. ROIC at the 94.5th percentile and margins at the 83rd are true but partly carry the D&A halving and a goodwill-light base, so I sit with the groups (82/70/76/64), above Tenaris and below Reply, whose market and reinvestment room are larger.

M:topic:4.reason: An honest tracker: no numerical EBITDAaL target missed, free cash flow guidance met with one 2% trim, EBITDA held through the energy shock, quarters within 0.3% of consensus and the FY2026 guide set above consensus and on track; but guidance has never been raised in a year under this CEO, it is conservative in its assumptions rather than its number, and consensus EPS has drifted slightly down over six months (-0.8% FY2026). M:topic:5.scale_version: the Rater v3.0, 2026-11-03: standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10), every item scored after the memo is written, the case first on judgement topics, anchors from the corrected ordering of 75 companies, the question groups' keys (D-SQ-280)

M:topic:5.letter_rule: rank within this item's population of the same scale (A top 10%, B next 15%, C, D and F quarters; B+, B, C+, C, C- sub-grades)
M:topic:5.reason: The structure has real gearing: 61-66% of cash costs fixed, incremental margins of about 95% on price and 60-80% on core volume (1% of core service revenue is about 2.2% of EPS), a CPI-linked clause on about two million postpaid contracts, a fibre lock-in loop and a buyback loop that turns flat net income into about 4% EPS growth. It is held to the 60s because pricing power is one year old and nominal, the gearing cuts both ways against cost inflation, the D&A tailwind is spent, financial leverage is nil (releveraging is an option the parent has called unpalatable), net cost-out is about 8 EURm a year, and the venture loop works against OTE; the forecast ratio is not meaningful with revenue falling on transit exit.

M:topic:5.letter_rule: rank within this item's population of the same scale (A top 10%, B next 15%, C, D and F quarters; B+, B, C+, C, C- sub-grades)
M:topic:5.reason: Several gears are proven and work together: about 215 USDm of a 420 USDm cash cost base is fixed and power is a nil-margin pass-through, so a colocation carries about 80% incremental EBITDA margin; a fixed 180 USDm finance charge, a dollar tax charge and buybacks cutting the share count about 15% turn FY2027-29 EBITDA growth of 16% into EPS growth of 55%, about three times; density and cash-return loops reinforce. Held below 90 because pricing is indexation-only with no real price rises and a latent downward direction at the DRC renewals, cost-out is small, and the 3.4-3.8x leverage and FX on intercompany loans make the same gearing bite on the downside.

M:topic:1.reason: External forces are a mild net positive over two to three years: the statutory wage shock is fading (net inflation drag down to £10m-12m), demand indicators are at records (pipeline £32.5bn, order intake +33%, renewals 91%) and regulation, decarbonisation, water and data centres give multi-year compliance and projects demand, but the UK market grows only 2-3%, the Public Interest Test reaches an exposed public book of about £800m-1bn from FY29, automation deflates hours-billed work and edge competition costs about 30bp on public renewals. Consensus sales growth at the 52nd percentile fits a typical, slightly positive environment; I agree with the group's 54 and lift it marginally for the margin relief in FY27-28, placing it just below Instalco's recovering end-market and above Tenaris's mixed one (the bid premium is not an operating-environment force and is not counted here).

M:topic:1.letter_rule: rank within this item's population of the same scale (A top 10%, B next 15%, C, D and F quarters; B+, B, C+, C, C- sub-grades)
M:topic:1.reason: External forces are a clear, multi-part, structural net positive on the 88% of revenue outside Exhibitions: professionals using AI still need trusted data, so database owners keep customers and charge more at renewal (peers confirm it: Thomson Reuters Legal at 9-10%, Karnov AI tiers at +30%), law-firm IT spend doubled from 2% to 4% of revenue, STM demand rose from 4% to 6%, and falling model and token costs help margins. Against that sit a funded and direct threat at the Legal workflow layer (Harvey, Legora, Google), a cyclical Middle East dip in Exhibitions and small grant-rule and print drags; consensus sales growth at the 75th percentile is honest, but group organic growth is steady at about 7% rather than accelerating, so this is above Spie's favourable-but-mixed reading and below Helios Towers' broad structural pull, a touch above the 66 External change forces group because the forces reach nearly the whole perimeter.

The structure is number one or two everywhere, with an 85-90% US legal-research duopoly, near-monopoly contributory data in Risk and unpaid or powerless suppliers. The moats (curated content licensed even by the entrants, retention above 95%) are widening under AI, and returns on new capital are above 30%, which the figures confirm (ROIC 24.8% at the 94th percentile, margins at the 82nd to 84th, cash conversion 99%) and which are among the most predictable in Europe. I sit above the 78-80 groups because all four are strong at once and predictability adds to the quality, and I deduct for the contested legal interface (about an eighth of profit), the limited room to reinvest and the open succession; that puts it above Reply and Avanza, well short of ASML's monopoly bottleneck.

M:topic:1.reason: Defence (47% of FY26 revenue) gets a funded, structural UK and NATO budget rise, and the 20/40/40 doctrine points it at Steatite's and Custom Power's products. The industrial destock has ended, and AI data-centre and US autonomy demand add a small third leg. These are offset by direct threats that are certain sooner: DRAM and component inflation, a £28bn Treasury funding gap with CMA screening that lengthens awards, the US continuing resolution, and unhedged dollar purchasing. I put it above the External change forces group (63) because this is a clear multi-part positive reaching most of sales, but below a 75 because the restock is a pulse and the defence money turns into contracts on a contested calendar.

M:topic:3.reason: Accreditation and design-in give a genuine but narrow moat on about 60% of revenue (Systems and Power). Against it: 39% is moatless distribution at a 4% margin, there is a sole-source channel dependency on Persistent with undisclosed terms, one customer is 17% of revenue, pricing power is only cost recovery, and the capacity built recently is under-used, so the return on new capital is still unproven. Low predictability keeps it in line with the groups (42 to 52), below IMCD's real specialty moat and above Teqnion's sub-par acquired returns.

M:topic:5.reason: Operating leverage is large and proven both ways. A £42m fixed overhead on a 33.5% gross margin puts break-even at about £110m to £115m; FY25's 23% revenue fall cut operating profit 65%, and each £10m of Systems revenue now adds about £3m of operating profit. The base case has EPS growing about 2.5 times as fast as revenue. It stays below 75 because the other gears are missing: pricing is only cost recovery, financial leverage is immaterial, cost-out is small and the loops are slow. And, as Richard warns, the gearing disappointed on the way up in FY26, when 70% of the gross-profit gain was reinvested in overhead.

M:topic:1.letter_rule: rank within this item's population of the same scale (A top 10%, B next 15%, C, D and F quarters; B+, B, C+, C, C- sub-grades)
M:topic:1.reason: A funded, regulated and multi-year external force reaches the core business: German transmission capex roughly triples at TenneT by 2027, allowed returns rise from 4.13% towards about 6.5%, and grid work is about a third of group revenue, with data centres, French nuclear and engineering outsourcing as further legs. Labour and 128-160-week equipment lead times cap it, so organic growth only rises from about 2.6% to 3-3.5%, and French fibre run-off, price-led French tertiary work and Global Services Energy take a fading slice. Consensus sales growth at the 50th percentile does not show it yet because the lag is mechanical. I go above the group's 64 because the force is written into regulation and contracts rather than forecast, but it reaches only part of sales, so it sits just below Eckert & Ziegler (72) and well above Odfjell Drilling (62).

M:topic:2.scale_version: the Rater v3.0, 2026-11-03: standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10), every item scored after the memo is written, the case first on judgement topics, anchors from the corrected ordering of 75 companies, the question groups' keys (D-SQ-280)

M:topic:2.letter_rule: rank within this item's population of the same scale (A top 10%, B next 15%, C, D and F quarters; B+, B, C+, C, C- sub-grades)
M:topic:2.reason: The company's own actions are clearly positive at EBITA: an orderly succession to the CEO who built Germany from EUR 650m to EUR 3.6bn, the 2028 margin target raised to 8.0% with EBITA above EUR 1bn, the largest acquisition year since 2017 (about EUR 800m of acquired revenue, about 8% of the group) and an investment-grade rating. Part of the gain is given back by the company's own choices: the ORNANE refinancing adds 2% to the share count and about EUR 30m of interest, so EPS lags EBITA by 2 to 3 points a year, and the new project-heavy segments have had overruns. That is more ambition than Richard's 'gently positive but mediocre' CVS (55) and close to OEM International's (66) turn into an active acquirer, but the dilution keeps it below that. I sit slightly above the group's 57 because the size of the acquisition step-up is itself a large change force.

M:topic:3.scale_version: the Rater v3.0, 2026-11-03: standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10), every item scored after the memo is written, the case first on judgement topics, anchors from the corrected ordering of 75 companies, the question groups' keys (D-SQ-280)
M:topic:3.note: set by the Rater; the Investment Analyst's own score was None
M:topic:3.letter_rule: rank within this item's population of the same scale (A top 10%, B next 15%, C, D and F quarters; B+, B, C+, C, C- sub-grades)
M:topic:3.reason: The qualitative parts are good but not exceptional. Germany is a fragmented market that SPIE consolidates and France is a rational oligopoly where SPIE is only number four. Moderate, mostly widening advantages come from prequalified grid and nuclear crews, a recruiting edge, frameworks with retention above 90%, and -34 days of working capital that funds growth. Management is disciplined but risk-averse, with organic growth averaging 1.8%. The Universe figures understate the financial profile: gross margin (pct 6), EBITDA margin (pct 19) and ROIC of 4.1% (pct 30) reflect a labour-services model and EUR 4.4bn of goodwill. Tenaris is number one in a three-player premium seamless oligopoly holding 84%, protected by mill-plus-qualification barriers and the Rig Direct procurement lock-in, with $3.56bn of net cash, capex near depreciation and a 20% EBITDA floor held through downturns. It is held back by cyclicality (EPS from -$0.54 to $3.32 in six years, so low predictability), by a margin lead over Vallourec that has gone, by a tariffed external steel supply and by controller-first governance. ROIC of 11.3% (p71) and about 15% mid-cycle on capital that now earns only about the old margin confirm a sound rather than elite profile. That places it with Volex-like quality, just under Theon, coherent with the groups' 64-74.

Its current half-year guide is conservative by construction, because realised prices lag a public index it already sees. I rate it above the groups' 62-64 because the repeatable beat mechanism and current conservatism are well evidenced.

M:topic:5.reason: Operating leverage is real and proven both ways: about 45% incremental margin on volume, a 4x price lever with 55-65% first-year drop-through (FY2027 +10% revenue gives +20% EBITDA), and a 25% fixed-cost cut delivered within three quarters in 2020. The company also holds a stable 34% price premium over the index. It falls short of the 75 level because the price it gears into is an industry rent it does not control, fixed costs ratchet up in upturns, there is no financial leverage (net cash), and the reinforcing loops give way to balancing ones from 2028. Even in the up year, EPS grows only about 1.4 times revenue.

M:topic:2.reason: The heart programme is the largest product entry in the company's history: CE-marked in August, the FDA PMA filed in September on category-best data, a three-tier European rollout. Alongside it come the liver 510(k) pivot, tenfold disposable capacity, abdominal consolidation in Sweden and the 2025 cost programme, which together justify 20%-plus revenue growth. Netted against them are a services unit losing money for six quarters (-19% gross margin), a CFO seat empty for eight months, a record of slipped dates, FlowHawk stalling, and launch costs that absorb the growth and keep 2027 EPS flat. That is a little lower than the 68 Richard ruled too high, and a few points above the group's 59 because a launch of this size is a large force whether or not it has reached earnings yet; it sits between OEM International (66) and Odfjell Drilling (61).
